nutshell: Person ReID models raise privacy concerns via unauthorized tracking, but unlike face recognition, ReID has no machine-unlearning technique to make a trained model 'forget' how to re-identify specific people while still working for everyone else. This paper defines the De-ReID problem and proposes variation-guided identity shift: push an unlearned person's original and style-augmented images apart in feature space (making their features sensitive to nuisance variation, i.e. not view-invariant) while pulling accessible persons' original/augmented pairs together (preserving view-invariance for them), plus a relation regularization term to stop the whole representation from collapsing.
contributions: First formalization of the De-ReID problem and a new benchmark (built from Market-1501, MSMT17, Occ-Duke, SYSU-MM01 splits) under a weakly-supervised setting: labeled images only for the persons to be unlearned, plus an unlabeled pool of accessible persons - deliberately avoiding the need for costly identity labels on everyone the model should keep working for.

Variation-guided identity shift (VIS): an asymmetric loss that pushes an unlearned person's image and its style-augmented view apart (biasing the model to encode nuisance/environmental cues for that identity) while pulling an accessible person's image and its augmented view together (preserving view-invariance) - shown via ablation to be more effective than naively separating an unlearned person's real cross-camera images directly, which the paper argues causes overfitting to training-time camera pairs.

Relation regularization: a triplet constraint that pushes an unlearned person's own images apart relative to their K-th nearest accessible-person neighbor, plus a consistency term that preserves the original model's pairwise similarity structure among accessible persons - the paper's own ablation shows the model collapses entirely without this consistency term (reported as '—' in Tables 6-7).

Broad empirical validation: beats adapted machine-unlearning baselines (GS-LoRA, LIRF, SCRUB, Boundary Shrink) and a naive camera-based label-augmentation baseline across 4 datasets, multiple unlearned-set sizes, and multiple ReID backbones (DCFormer, PAT, PHA); notably, competing unlearning methods' protection is largely undone by standard Re-Ranking post-processing, while this method's H-Mean actually improves under Re-Ranking.
deficiencies: The method doesn't drive re-identification of 'unlearned' persons to near-zero in harder settings - e.g. 13.1% Rank-1 still succeeds at MT=100 in MSMT17, and 12-18% Rank-1 when applied to other backbones (Table 5) - which is a real gap for a method framed around preventing people from being re-identified, since a meaningful fraction of query attempts still succeed.

Performance depends on having a sizeable unlabeled pool of accessible persons at fine-tuning time, and the paper's own ablation (Table 8) shows H-Mean drops from 66.7% to 57.6% as that pool shrinks from 141 to 60 people - a realistic small-scale deployment (e.g. a household or single business wanting to forget one person) may not have such a pool available, and the paper only partially compensates for this with an external dataset (LUPerson) rather than showing the method holds up under genuinely scarce unlabeled data.

The relation-consistency regularizer (L_RCR) explicitly constrains accessible-person relations to match the original pretrained model, meaning the method by design cannot improve ReID accuracy on accessible persons and in practice costs several points of Rank-1 (e.g. 96.3% -> 84.4%-91.1% in Market-1501) - this accuracy cost to the 'protected' majority of users is a real trade-off that isn't discussed as a limitation anywhere in the paper.

The evaluation protocol only tests cross-camera matching of unlearned persons (images from disjoint cameras in train vs. test); since the method's mechanism relies on making unlearned-person features sensitive to style/environmental variation rather than removing identity information outright, it's untested whether an attacker with images of the same 'unlearned' person under similar lighting/camera conditions (rather than a different camera) could still successfully match them - a more direct test of whether identity is actually forgotten versus merely made view-variant.
notable: A genuinely useful finding for anyone evaluating privacy claims in this space: standard Re-Ranking post-processing - a common, off-the-shelf ReID accuracy booster - reverses the unlearning effect of every competing baseline (e.g. SCRUB's unlearned-person Rank-1 rises from 43.8% to 52.3% after re-ranking), meaning those methods only disrupt the single nearest match while leaving enough residual identity signal in the broader neighborhood structure for a common post-processing step to recover it. Any 'unlearning' or de-identification result reported only on raw Rank-1, without checking against re-ranking, should be treated with suspicion given this result. Also notable: the paper makes a clear conceptual argument for why classification-style machine unlearning methods (which target decision boundaries or network weights) don't transfer to metric-learning/retrieval tasks like ReID - a person can still be correctly retrieved via feature distance even if they'd be misclassified - which is a useful distinction for applying unlearning techniques across task types generally, not just ReID.
